note.note:
HISTORY & PHYSICAL (DETAILED)

Consult Summary:
28-year-old woman with no prior headache history presents via telehealth with a 24-hour history of left-sided posterior throbbing headache rated 8/10; no red-flag features elicited and clinician advised trial of stronger NSAID plus paracetamol, rest, hydration, and safety-net for worsening or new symptoms.

History:
• Presenting complaint: New-onset headache.  
• Onset: Yesterday mid-morning; gradual build-up over a short period.  
• Location/character: Left posterior/occipital; throbbing, “intense.”  
• Severity: 8/10.  
• Duration/progression: Persistent over the past day; no diurnal or positional variation.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, phonophobia, limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, fever, chills, neck stiffness, rash.  
• Triggers/relievers: Single dose of ibuprofen (Nurofen) provided little relief; no change with posture, activity, or Valsalva.  
• Function: Able to work but with difficulty.  
• Review of systems otherwise unremarkable.

Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  

Medications:
• Ibuprofen (Nurofen) – single dose yesterday; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• No regular prescription or over-the-counter medications.  

Allergies:
• No known drug, food, or environmental allergies reported.

Social History:
• Lives with partner.  
• Occupation: Designer (desk-based).  
• Tobacco: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: Denies use.  
• Recreational drugs: Denies use.

Family History:
• Mother: Hypertension and migraines.  
• No other familial conditions reported.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (telehealth).  
• General/Neurological/Ophthalmologic/Meningeal exams: Not performed; no objective findings available.

Investigations:
• None ordered or reviewed during this encounter.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
New-onset unilateral throbbing headache without red-flag features; most consistent with a primary headache disorder (probable migraine without aura vs tension-type), but early course requires close follow-up.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Migraine without aura – Unilateral throbbing 8/10, functional impairment, positive family history; opposing: first-ever headache, no nausea/photophobia.  
2. Tension-type headache – Common, lacks focal/neuro signs; opposing: unilateral throbbing, high severity.  
3. Cervicogenic headache – Occipital unilateral pain in desk worker; opposing: no neck pain or positional component.

Issue 1 – Acute new-onset headache:
Assessment:
• Likely primary headache (migraine vs tension-type); no current features suggesting secondary intracranial pathology, but first presentation warrants vigilance.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Prescribed a stronger NSAID (name/dose not documented) to be taken regularly with food; may use paracetamol concomitantly.  
• Supportive: Rest, adequate hydration.  
• Safety-net: Seek urgent care if headache worsens, fails to improve within 1–2 days, or if new symptoms arise (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, visual changes, focal neurological deficits).  
• Follow-up: Contact clinic in 1–2 days if no improvement or sooner for red-flag symptoms. Consider in-person visit with vitals and neurological exam if persistent.

General Plan Items:
• Encourage patient to monitor triggers/stress; keep headache diary if recurrent.  
• Recommend blood pressure check at next opportunity given family history of hypertension.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vital signs, neurological or fundoscopic examination, or blood pressure recorded.  
• No contradictions between transcript and DDx noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; telehealth limitations precluded physical exam.
